q: Origin law in Europe reaches from the line on the map through the vineyard and into the cellar. Which of these does it leave entirely to the producer?
opts: The maximum yield per hectare
The minimum alcoholic strength at picking
The grape varieties that may be planted
The price at which the wine is sold
exp: A denomination governs how wine is grown and made, not what it costs or who may buy it, so bottles from one village can sit ten times apart on the same list. Price control has been tried historically and is now vanishingly rare, since it turns a quality rulebook into a cartel.

q: European law will not let a bottle print a single grape name unless eighty-five percent of the wine is that grape, and American federal law asks for less than that. What does it ask for?
opts: Fifty-one percent of the wine
The same eighty-five percent that Europe asks
Seventy-five percent of the wine
Ninety percent of the wine
exp: A quarter of an American varietal wine may be something else entirely, and none of it need be declared anywhere, so a varietal label is a majority claim rather than a purity claim on either side of the Atlantic. The federal figure is a floor rather than a settlement: individual states may hold their own growers above it and several do, while no European appellation may go below the European figure.

q: A cask in a European cellar is topped up each year from the harvest that follows, and the producer still means to print one year on the label. How much of the wine may come from other years?
opts: None of it whatever
Twenty-five percent of the volume
Fifteen percent of the volume
Five percent of the volume
exp: European rules ask that eighty-five percent of a bottle carrying a year come from that harvest, and the margin exists so that a small topping-up from an adjacent year does not cost a wine its vintage. Other countries set their own figures, so a producer selling into several markets has to work to the strictest of them rather than to the rule at home. It matters most for wines held in cask and drawn on gradually, and a wine that cannot meet the figure simply goes out without a year on it.

q: A laboratory in Bordeaux finds 13.9 percent alcohol in a bottle whose label states 13.5 percent, and no offence has been committed. Why not?
opts: The labelled strength carries a legal tolerance of half a percentage point
Tolerance applies only to wines sold outside the country of production
Any figure is lawful provided it has been rounded downward
Alcohol statements are advisory and carry no legal force
exp: Alcohol varies from vat to vat and analysis carries its own error, so labels are printed to a permitted margin either side of the true figure rather than to a measurement. A wider tolerance is allowed for certain categories, including some wines matured for years before release, which is why two identically labelled bottles can genuinely differ. The half point is the European figure, and American rules allow a wider margin again.

q: Wine bottles arrive in a fixed set of sizes and never in, say, 600 millilitres. What accounts for that?
opts: Duty is chargeable only on those particular volumes, so no other size is worth filling
Law prescribes the nominal volumes in which wine may be sold
Glassmakers settled on a voluntary industry standard
Cork diameters limit the range of usable bottle necks
exp: The permitted list runs from small aircraft measures through the half and the standard bottle up to the magnum, above which European law simply stops prescribing, and it is consumer-protection law of the same family as net-quantity marking on any packaged good. A producer cannot invent a size to frustrate a price comparison on the shelf.

q: A grower brings in more fruit than his appellation's permitted yield allows. What becomes of the surplus?
opts: It goes out under a lower name, not the appellation
The grower forfeits the appellation for his next three vintages
It must be left unharvested on the vine and written off
It may be sold under the appellation name at a reduced price once the surplus has been declared
exp: The sanction attaches to the name rather than to the wine, so the surplus goes out under a lower designation or to the still, and nothing is wasted or smuggled through. Push past the absolute ceiling that many rulebooks set above the permitted yield and the penalty is heavier still, since the whole of that year's crop loses the name rather than the excess alone. Rules of this kind are why a wet, generous year shows up in a region's paperwork as much as in its cellars.

q: Denominazione, Denominacion, Denominacao and Appellation all appear on European labels in four different languages. What single idea do all four express?
opts: That the name is a designation of origin
That the wine passed a government tasting panel
That the wine was matured in oak before release
That the estate grew the fruit and bottled the wine on its own premises
exp: All four are the local word for naming, each of them fixed by law, three built on Latin nomen and the French on appellare, and all four wines sit in the same European category whatever the spelling. What follows the word is what tells you which national rung is meant.

q: An estate makes one of its country's most admired and expensive reds and sells it under the humblest geographical tier available. What does that reveal about the tiers?
opts: The tiers rank producers by reputation, so a famous estate sits at the top of them
A tier records only compliance with a rulebook
The estate has been demoted for a breach of the rules
The wine must in fact be of modest quality
exp: A producer who wants a grape or a technique the local rulebook forbids has to accept the lower name, and buyers who follow producers rather than appellations do not care. Several of the most sought-after wines in Europe are sold exactly this way, which is the strongest practical argument against reading a tier as a quality score.

q: A celebrated property asks to have its own wines raised to the national top tier while its neighbours stay where they are. Why does that request normally fail?
opts: Only the state may initiate a promotion, never a producer
The tier is granted to a delimited area and not to a company
Top tiers are closed to privately owned estates
The applicant must first be ranked by an independent tasting panel drawn from outside the region
exp: Promotion is a decision about ground, so one estate's excellence argues for its whole appellation and never for itself alone. A few countries have created a category for a single property, and it is a deliberate exception written precisely because the general rule works the other way.

q: Greece, Bulgaria and Romania all print the same pair of European origin categories on their labels as France and Italy do. What made that so?
opts: All three adopted the categories voluntarily, judging that European wording would help their exports
The World Trade Organization allocated the categories to them
All three signed a bilateral treaty with France
All are European Union members, so one framework applies
exp: The framework comes with membership rather than being an option a country weighs up. It means a Greek designation and a French one are the same legal object in different languages, which is why a sommelier can read the standing of a label from a country whose alphabet they cannot.

q: One European country built its quality ladder on how much sugar the fruit carried at picking rather than on how tightly the boundary was drawn. Which country?
opts: Portugal
France
Italy
Germany
exp: It is the deepest structural difference in European wine law: a ripeness ladder can be climbed anywhere in the country, while an origin ladder cannot be climbed at all, only inhabited. It also means the most prominent quality word on such a label says nothing whatever about which vineyard the wine came from.

q: Wine rules in one Alpine country are written canton by canton, so the yield ceiling for the same grape changes as you cross a lake. Which country?
opts: Austria
Slovenia
Liechtenstein
Switzerland
exp: A federal layer sets the outline and each canton fills in appellations, ceilings and ripeness minimums for itself. The fragmentation is one reason so little of the wine is seen abroad, since no single national name ever gathered enough recognition to sell on.

q: A ladder built on sugar at harvest is steadily losing its power to separate one wine from another as the growing season warms. Why?
opts: The middle rungs are now reached in most years, so they stop separating
European law now forbids ladders based on must weight
Growers deliberately pick unripe to avoid the higher rungs
Must weight can no longer be measured accurately in warm conditions
exp: A rung means something only while it is hard to reach, and warming has made the middle of such a ladder attainable in most sites in most years. That pressure is why growers' associations built vineyard hierarchies of their own from the 1990s, and why a ripeness ladder is now typically set alongside an origin pyramid that narrows from a region through a sub-region and a village down to a single vineyard, rather than being replaced by one.

q: Letters on a Canadian label stand for an alliance whose rules reach past simply tracing where the fruit grew. What else does it require?
opts: That the wine be aged in Canadian oak
That the wine be held a minimum of two years before release
That the wine pass a laboratory test and a tasting panel
That the producer own every vineyard the fruit came from rather than buying any of it in
exp: A wine has to clear an expert panel as well as the laboratory before it is released. The Vintners Quality Alliance also fixes minimum ripeness and a list of permitted varieties, which puts it much closer to a European appellation than to most schemes in the New World. It is a useful corrective to the idea that the two hemispheres regulate wine in fundamentally different ways.

q: Before rules settled in 2015, a bottle sold as Japanese wine could be made from imported bulk juice and never see a Japanese grape. What did those rules require?
opts: That the grape variety always be stated on the front label
That every bottle carry a tasting panel number
That imported juice be capped at fifteen percent of any blend sold at home
That Japan Wine must be from grapes grown there
exp: Wine bottled domestically from foreign juice now has to say so, which separated a small quality sector from a large blending trade at a stroke. The standard was set in 2015 and came into force three years later, after a transition that let the old labels run out. It is a recent instance of the oldest idea in wine law: make the label say where the fruit actually grew.

q: Several countries outside Europe agreed by treaty to stop using European place names as style words for their own fortified and sparkling wines. What did that oblige them to do?
opts: Pay a licence fee to the European producers concerned
Restrict those wines to their own domestic markets
Invent or adopt new names for those styles
Stop making those styles altogether
exp: It is geographical-indication protection in its most practical form: a word treated as a style description for a century turned out to belong to somebody else. Some of the replacement terms have since become respected names in their own right, which was not obvious at the time.
